title: Boss: the bad afternoon
summary: Undo the right way in five real situations, then build the undo tools yourself.

steps.title: The scene
body: It is 4 p.m. on a busy day and everything goes wrong at once: a wrong commit message, a commit that broke `main` for everyone, a `reset --hard` typed into the wrong terminal, and a half-finished feature in the way of a hotfix.
For each one, pick the undo that fits: **is it pushed?** and **is it committed?** are the two questions that decide.

steps.prompt: You pushed `Add audit log` to `main` this morning. It turns out to leak user emails into the logs. Teammates have pulled. What do you do?
options: `git revert <hash>`, push, and then fix forward on a branch
`git commit --amend` to remove the logging, then push
Ask everyone to delete their clones
steps.explain: Shared history only grows. Revert is the safe, auditable undo. (If the leak exposed data, also handle the incident: the logs themselves need cleaning.)

steps.prompt: Your branch `cart` was `A---B---C---D`. You typed `git reset --hard HEAD~3` by mistake, then made one new commit `E`. What does `git reflog` show for `HEAD@{2}`? Answer with the commit letter.
code: git reset --hard HEAD~3   # cart now at A
git commit -m "E"         # cart now at E (parent A)
git reflog                # HEAD@{0}: commit E, HEAD@{1}: reset, HEAD@{2}: ?
steps.explain: `HEAD@{0}` is E, `HEAD@{1}` is where the reset landed (A), and `HEAD@{2}` is before the reset: D. `git branch recovered HEAD@{2}` gets B, C and D back.

steps.title: Undo advisor
prompt: Write `Advise(bool committed, bool pushed, bool keepChanges)` returning the command a senior engineer would suggest to undo **the last change**:
`-` means the value does not matter.
starter: static string Advise(bool committed, bool pushed, bool keepChanges)
solution: static string Advise(bool committed, bool pushed, bool keepChanges)
return keepChanges ? "git reset --soft HEAD~1" : "git reset --hard HEAD~1";
hints: Pushed commits always get `revert`, whatever `keepChanges` says.
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("uncommitted, keep", "git restore --staged .", Advise(false, false, true));
Dojo.Eq("uncommitted, discard", "git restore .", Advise(false, true, false));
Dojo.Eq("pushed, keep", "git revert HEAD", Advise(true, true, true));
Dojo.Eq("pushed, discard", "git revert HEAD", Advise(true, true, false));
Dojo.Eq("local, keep", "git reset --soft HEAD~1", Advise(true, false, true));
Dojo.Eq("local, discard", "git reset --hard HEAD~1", Advise(true, false, false));

steps.title: Reset, then rescue
prompt: Put two models together. Write `Rescue(string mode, string target, state, snapshot, string beforeReset)`:
2. Then recover with `git reset --hard <beforeReset>`: apply `Reset("--hard", beforeReset, ...)` to the result.
Include your `Reset` method. Notice in the tests what the rescue **cannot** bring back: the uncommitted edit.
starter: static (string Tip, string Index, string Work) Rescue(string mode, string target, (string Tip, string Index, string Work) state, Dictionary<string, string> snapshot, string beforeReset)
solution: static (string Tip, string Index, string Work) Reset(string mode, string target, (string Tip, string Index, string Work) state, Dictionary<string, string> snapshot)
static (string Tip, string Index, string Work) Rescue(string mode, string target, (string Tip, string Index, string Work) state, Dictionary<string, string> snapshot, string beforeReset)
var afterMistake = Reset(mode, target, state, snapshot);
hints: The second call starts from the first call's result.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoSnap = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["A"] = "v1", ["D"] = "v4" };
var dojoStart = ("D", "v4", "v4+uncommitted");
Dojo.Eq("the commit comes back, the uncommitted edit does not", ("D", "v4", "v4"), Rescue("--hard", "A", dojoStart, dojoSnap, "D"));
Dojo.Eq("after a soft reset the rescue lands in the same place", ("D", "v4", "v4"), Rescue("--soft", "A", dojoStart, dojoSnap, "D"));

steps.title: Revert a whole series
steps.prompt: `git revert C B` reverts several commits, newest first, each on top of the last result. Write `RevertMany(current, List<(Dictionary<string,string> Parent, Dictionary<string,string> Child)> commits)` that applies your `Revert` from lesson 4 for each commit **in the order given**, feeding each result into the next. Collect every conflict path (in order, no duplicates). Include `Revert`.
starter: static (Dictionary<string, string> Result, List<string> Conflicts) RevertMany(Dictionary<string, string> current, List<(Dictionary<string, string> Parent, Dictionary<string, string> Child)> commits)
solution: static (Dictionary<string, string> Result, List<string> Conflicts) Revert(Dictionary<string, string> current, Dictionary<string, string> parent, Dictionary<string, string> child)
foreach (var path in parent.Keys.Union(child.Keys).OrderBy(p => p, StringComparer.Ordinal))
if (before is null) result.Remove(path); else result[path] = before;
static (Dictionary<string, string> Result, List<string> Conflicts) RevertMany(Dictionary<string, string> current, List<(Dictionary<string, string> Parent, Dictionary<string, string> Child)> commits)
foreach (var x in conflicts) if (!all.Contains(x)) all.Add(x);
hints: Keep a running `current` and reassign it after each `Revert`.
template: {{CODE}}
string dojoS(Dictionary<string, string> d) => string.Join(",", d.OrderBy(k => k.Key, StringComparer.Ordinal).Select(k => k.Key + "=" + k.Value));
var sA = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["f"] = "1" };
var sB = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["f"] = "2" };
var sC = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["f"] = "3", ["g"] = "x" };
var (r, c) = RevertMany(new(sC), new() { (sB, sC), (sA, sB) });
Dojo.Eq("revert C then B gets back to A", "f=1", dojoS(r));
Dojo.Eq("no conflicts in the right order", new List<string>(), c);
var (r2, c2) = RevertMany(new(sC), new() { (sA, sB), (sB, sC) });
Dojo.Eq("oldest first conflicts on f", new List<string> { "f" }, c2);
